reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that shyness emerges from a conflict between internal self-models and external social expectations. The first primitive, Social Attention Entropy, captures how stranger encounters increase cognitive load through attentional conflict—akin to information-theoretic entropy in communication channels. As strangers become more authoritative or novel, this entropy grows, leading to behavioral inhibition. The second primitive, Self-Model Confidence, formalizes the idea that confidence in one’s social self is context-dependent, decaying in unfamiliar settings. This mirrors Bayesian belief updating under uncertain priors. The third primitive, Blush Response Function, maps physiological indicators into a dynamic model of arousal, where eye aversion and body awkwardness are symptoms of high-stakes self-evaluation. These three primitives form a triadic system: entropy drives uncertainty, confidence modulates belief, and physiological response reflects the outcome. Failure modes include cognitive overload, where H_S exceeds capacity, or complete collapse of C_self, leading to paralysis. Dualities arise in the distinction between fear (which is reactive) and shyness (which is anticipatory), and the interplay between internal consistency and external validation. The system is non-linear, with thresholds triggering cascading effects in behavior.
